manifold

/MAN-uh-fohld/ - the stress falls on MAN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Manifold means many and of many different kinds; varied.

Her objections to the merger were manifold, running from the price to the timing to the fate of the night shift.

Example

Why did families join the 1889 land rush? The historian's card file gives manifold answers: debts in Ohio, drought in Texas, a brother already out there, a newspaper's promise of free quarter-sections, and, on one card, simply 'tired of fences.' No two wagons rolled west for quite the same reason.

Manifold is more exact than 'numerous' because it counts kinds as well as heads: many and of many different varieties. Fifty identical complaints would be numerous; fifty different ones are manifold. The word is formal and a little stately — the everyday phrase is 'all kinds of.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

assorted: Assorted means of mixed kinds gathered casually together — assorted chocolates, assorted screws in a jar; it is a grab-bag word for physical collections. Manifold is formal and abstract, describing reasons, uses, or objections that are both many and varied. A drawer holds assorted odds and ends; a treaty has manifold consequences.

myriad: Myriad means so many that counting them is hopeless — the myriad stars over a desert — and it speaks only to number. Manifold makes a double claim: many, and of many different kinds, even for a set small enough to count. Ten thousand identical bolts are myriad; five unlike reasons are manifold.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

single: one, and only one

few: small in number, however alike or different

Where it sits · how high the count and how varied

several → numerous → manifold

several vs. manifold: Several is a modest handful — three or four — nowhere near manifold.

numerous vs. manifold: Numerous goes further than several, piling up the count, but it stops short of manifold, which adds that the many things are of many different kinds.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mani: many (Old English manig)

Root — fold: times, multiplied (Old English -fald)

Put it together: Mani (many) + fold (times over) = many times over. This is native English, a thousand years old: manigfeald described blessings, sorrows, and gifts that came many-fold — multiplied and various at once. Its Latin-built twin is 'multiple,' but manifold keeps the older, statelier ring.

Use the root in a new word: tenfold: The registrar refused to publish the tenfold figure until she had checked it herself.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Manifold suits formal prose — reports, sermons, ceremony: 'the benefits are manifold.' In this unit, keep it apart from multifaceted: manifold describes many varied things (reasons, uses, objections), while multifaceted describes one thing with many sides. For everyday speech, 'all kinds of' does the same work.
